content: Rotylenchulus reniformis is a nematode, a type of roundworm, belonging to the family Hoplolaimidae. It is commonly referred to as the reniform nematode due to the characteristic kidney-shaped appearance of the female, which curls her exposed posterior while feeding. This nematode is a significant plant parasite, attacking a wide range of crops and other plants. In parasitology, it is classified as a cyst-forming nematode that primarily targets the roots of its host plants. Rotylenchulus reniformis thrives in sandy loamy soils. Life Cycle Rotylenchulus reniformis exhibits both ectoparasitic (living on the surface of the plant) and semi-endoparasitic (partially inside the plant) behaviors. Male nematodes are ectoparasitic and are generally considered non-pathogenic, as they do not significantly affect the plant. Female nematodes, however, penetrate the roots of the host plant and form cysts, leaving part of their body (the posterior) exposed outside the root. This exposed portion facilitates copulation and egg-laying. After mating, the female lays approximately 30 to 75 eggs outside the root in a gelatinous matrix. This matrix serves to keep the eggs moist and protects them from predation by other organisms. The eggs hatch within 8 to 10 days, and the larvae undergo three to four molts before developing into adult males and females. Notably, only the females have been observed feeding. The complete life cycle of Rotylenchulus reniformis is completed within 17 to 23 days. Disease Symptoms Rotylenchulus reniformis induces hypertrophy in the pericycle cells of root seedlings and in the periderm cells of the roots of plants that are 4 to 5 weeks old. Infected plants exhibit reduced root growth, with fewer large roots and an abundance of coarse, stubby lateral roots. Diseased plants may become severely stunted, chlorotic (yellowed), and prone to wilting. Wilting is often exacerbated by opportunistic pathogens, such as Fusarium wilt in cotton. Root decay is typically caused by secondary fungal infections. Control Chemical control measures applied prior to planting are effective in managing Rotylenchulus reniformis populations. Crop rotation is relatively ineffective, as this nematode can parasitize the roots of most crops. In irrigated areas, allowing the field to dry out for a year can significantly reduce the presence of Rotylenchulus reniformis and other nematodes. Biological control methods, such as the use of Paecilomyces lilacinus, a fungal egg parasite, have also been employed. Distribution Rotylenchulus reniformis is distributed worldwide, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions, including Texas and the southeastern United States. It has a wide range of host plants, including fruit trees, lentils, cotton, cowpea, pigeon pea, tea, tobacco, soybean, pineapple, bananas, sweet potato, alfalfa, corn, asparagus, palm, cucumber, squash, melon, and ginger.
